candidate.name: Oachira Parabrahma Temple
candidate.reason: Pilgrims and heritage travellers explore this rare open-air, idol-less temple known as Dakshina Kashi with unique rituals and martial displays.

claims.claim: Oachira Parabrahma Temple occupies approximately 36 acres of open ground (figures in sources range around this value).
Nearest railway station: Kayamkulam Junction, about 11 km away.

Oachirakkali originated as annual war-exercises performed by soldiers of the Kayamkulam Raja; the padanilam served as their practice ground. Traditional/local accounts describe participation by soldiers from the region’s karas and kalaries.
Early 19th century: British surveyors Ward and Conner documented the Padanilam ground and central reservoir (chira) linked to the Kayamkulam (Odanattu/Onattu) Raja.

results.claim: Oachira Parabrahma Temple occupies approximately 36 acres of open ground (figures in sources range around this value).
results.evidence: I could not retrieve the cited Kerala Tourism PDF at that URL. The temple's official site and multiple tourism sites state the pilgrimage centre "covers thirty six acres of land." (e.g. https://oachiraparabrahmatemple.org/oachira-temple and Wikipedia). However, a December 3, 2024 Supreme Court record and reputable legal reports record the legally recorded area as 21.25 acres (see court reporting / judgment summaries such as https://indiankanoon.org/doc/60501045/ and https://www.livelaw.in/amp/supreme-court/.../277177). The tourism/temple sources support '36 acres'; the court judgment contradicts it with 21.25 acres.
results.fix: Report both figures and cite sources: e.g. “Many temple and tourism sources state the compound is about 36 acres (see temple website and tourism pages); however the Supreme Court of India recorded the temple’s area as 21.25 acres in its December 3, 2024 judgment. Cite the court judgment for the legally recorded extent and note the discrepancy.”

results.claim: Nearest railway station: Kayamkulam Junction, about 11 km away.
results.evidence: Kerala Tourism 'Getting there' entry: “Nearest railway station: Kayamkulam Junction, about 11 kms away.” (https://www.keralatourism.org/temples/kollam/oachira)

results.claim: Oachirakkali originated as annual war-exercises performed by soldiers of the Kayamkulam Raja; the padanilam served as their practice ground. Traditional/local accounts describe participation by soldiers from the region’s karas and kalaries.
results.evidence: The Kerala Tourism Oachirakkali festival sheet links the festival to the battle of Kayamkulam, describes the Padanilam/battlefield next to the temple and states the mock battle is enacted by trained warriors representing local karas, headed by 'Kalari Ashans'. (https://www.keralatourism.org/1000festivals/assets/uploads/pdf/1530899547-0.pdf)

results.claim: Early 19th century: British surveyors Ward and Conner documented the Padanilam ground and central reservoir (chira) linked to the Kayamkulam (Odanattu/Onattu) Raja; they noted a large reservoir used by soldiers for bathing and watering horses, and a very old damaged pagoda on the eastern side of the Padanilam.
results.evidence: The Wikipedia article reports that Ward & Conner (early-19th-century Travancore surveyors) observed a central chira used by soldiers for bathing and watering horses and a very old damaged temple on the eastern side of the Padanilam. However, that Wikipedia section is uncited and no direct quotation from the Ward & Conner memoir was provided on the page. I located library/catalog records for the Ward & Conner 'Memoir of the Survey of the Travancore and Cochin States' (the likely primary source) but did not find an accessible digitised page-quote in this check.
results.fix: Retain the historical claim only with a primary or reliable secondary citation. Replace the Wikipedia reference with a direct citation to the Ward & Conner memoir (Memoir of the Survey of the Travancore and Cochin States) with page number, or cite a reputable secondary source (state manuals, academic work) that reproduces the Ward & Conner passage. If the primary text cannot be located, reword to indicate it is reported in secondary sources: e.g. “Early-19th-century Travancore surveyors Ward & Conner are reported to have recorded… (cite the memoir or a scholarly source that quotes it).”

issues.problem: Authoritative legal record (Supreme Court judgment, Dec 3, 2024) gives the temple area as 21.25 acres which contradicts the commonly-repeated '36 acres' figure used in the entry.
issues.suggestion: Present both figures with sources; use the court judgment for the legally recorded extent and cite it. Avoid an unqualified single acreage figure.

issues.problem: The statement that Ward & Conner documented the Padanilam/chira presently cites Wikipedia; the relevant Wikipedia text is uncited. Historical documentary claims need the primary Ward & Conner memoir or a reliable secondary source.
issues.suggestion: Locate and cite the Ward & Conner 'Memoir of the Survey of the Travancore and Cochin States' (with page reference), or cite a reputable academic/state history that quotes the memoir. If not available, clearly mark the statement as reported/uncorroborated rather than documentary fact.

issues.problem: Statements about inclusivity, dress, photography and 'no fixed entry fee' are reasonable but lack sourcing. Rules around photography, dress and footwear can vary and are sensitive for visitors.
issues.suggestion: Add a caveat and cite official temple rules or Kerala Tourism/temple site guidance. Where no official rule is available, advise visitors to check on arrival.

issues.problem: The folklore section attributes the legend to 'Aithihyamala and local tradition' which is appropriate, but the entry does not cite a source for the Aithihyamala reference.
issues.suggestion: Cite the Aithihyamala volume or a reliable secondary source that records the Akavoor Chathan legend, or state explicitly when the legend is 'local tradition' if primary citation is not available.

verification.folkloreAssessment: Good. The entry frames the bull/Chathan story as local legend and attributes it to Aithihyamala and local tradition rather than presenting it as historical fact. This hedging and attribution are appropriate. Recommend adding a direct citation to the Aithihyamala passage or another published source that records the tale.
verification.sensitivityAssessment: Generally respectful and neutral. The entry avoids derogatory language and frames inclusivity positively. Sensitive operational claims (entry rules, dress, photography, 'open to all castes and faiths') should be sourced or worded as guidance to avoid implying official policy where none is cited. No stereotyping observed.
